title: State v. McDonald
description: Whether Christopher McDonald's 80-year sentence for first-degree robbery is constitutionally disproportionate and whether the circuit court erred in denying his motion to withdraw his guilty plea, which was based on the argument that a BB gun is not a 'firearm or other deadly weapon' for first-degree robbery.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the circuit court correctly denied the motion to withdraw the guilty plea because it exceeded the scope of the limited remand, and that the 80-year sentence for first-degree robbery is constitutionally proportionate.
defendant_argument: Christopher McDonald argued that his 80-year sentence is constitutionally disproportionate and that the circuit court erred in denying his motion to withdraw his guilty plea because a BB gun is not a 'firearm or other deadly weapon' under the first-degree robbery statute.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's resentencing order, upholding the 80-year sentence and the denial of the motion to withdraw the guilty plea.

title: State v. Small
description: Whether Richard Small's constitutional due process rights were violated during his trial by his absence from critical-stage hearings, the admission of prejudicial evidence, the failure to sever his trial, the denial of his motion to suppress his statement, and improper prosecutorial remarks.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the circuit court did not err on any of the points raised by Mr. Small, and his convictions and sentence should be affirmed.
defendant_argument: Mr. Small argued that his due process rights were violated, entitling him to a new trial or suppression of evidence, due to his absence from critical hearings, the admission of prejudicial gang evidence, the failure to sever his trial, the improper denial of his motion to suppress his statement, and the State's improper comments on his right to remain silent during closing arguments.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Mr. Small's convictions and sentence for conspiracy to commit first-degree murder and first-degree murder.

title: State v. Cohee
description: Whether the circuit court erred in refusing to impose a recidivist life sentence on Mr. McGann, with the State arguing the court lacked discretion to deviate from the mandatory sentence, and Mr. McGann arguing the life sentence would be unconstitutionally disproportionate or arbitrarily applied.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the circuit court lacked the authority to impose any sentence other than a recidivist life sentence because the relevant statute uses the mandatory word "shall," and the court's decision was clearly erroneous as a matter of law.
defendant_argument: Mr. McGann argued that a recidivist life sentence would violate the proportionality clause of the West Virginia Constitution and that the State's application of the recidivist statutes was arbitrary and capricious, thus violating substantive due process.
decision_outcome: The court granted the State's writ of prohibition, ordering the circuit court to impose a recidivist life sentence on Mr. McGann.

title: In re S.M.
description: Whether the circuit court erred by terminating the petitioner's parental rights and by accepting his stipulation to abuse and neglect allegations without the presence of counsel.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner argued that the circuit court erred by accepting his stipulation to abuse and neglect allegations without his attorney present and by terminating his parental rights, contending he should have been given another chance for rehabilitation.
defendant_argument: The Department of Human Services (DHS) argued that the circuit court did not err because the petitioner knowingly and intelligently waived his right to counsel and was given multiple opportunities to correct the conditions of abuse and neglect but failed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Appeals affirmed the circuit court's order terminating the petitioner's parental rights.

title: Norwood v. Frame
description: Whether Travis Norwood's life recidivist sentence for heroin trafficking violates equal protection principles due to disparate treatment compared to a similar case involving oxycodone trafficking.
plaintiff_argument: Norwood argues his life recidivist sentence violates equal protection principles because it results in disparate treatment compared to the Lane case, where a similar drug offense (oxycodone) led to a reversed life sentence, despite statutory law treating both drugs similarly for sentencing.
defendant_argument: The court (implicitly the defendant's stance) argues that Norwood's sentence is not unconstitutionally disproportionate, distinguishing heroin trafficking due to its inherent risk of violence and societal impact, and asserting that judicial discretion in sentencing does not violate due process or equal protection.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's order denying the petitioner's second petition for a writ of habeas corpus.

title: Roman Realty, LLC v. The City of Morgantown
description: Whether a property owner can compel a municipality to institute eminent domain proceedings for property damages, or if a civil tort action provides an adequate alternative remedy for just compensation.
plaintiff_argument: Roman Realty, LLC argued that tort actions do not provide an adequate remedy for property damages, they are entitled to an impartial jury of twelve freeholders, and attorney's fees are unavailable in tort cases but recoverable in mandamus proceedings, thus requiring eminent domain proceedings.
defendant_argument: The City of Morgantown argued that Roman Realty had another adequate remedy at law, specifically a civil action in tort, which precludes the issuance of a writ of mandamus.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's order granting summary judgment to the City of Morgantown, finding that Roman Realty failed to meet its burden to establish the absence of another adequate remedy.

title: State v. Slaughter
description: Whether the Circuit Court of Fayette County erred in crediting the defendant only thirty days of time served instead of the entire 263-day period he was incarcerated, thereby infringing on his constitutional rights under the due process and double jeopardy clauses of the West Virginia Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Circuit Court of Fayette County's decision to credit only thirty days was proper under State v. Taylor, contending that once the defendant's bond was revoked on Raleigh County charges, he began serving time on those charges, justifying the deferral of credit assignment to Raleigh County.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that he should have received credit for the entire 263-day period he was incarcerated on the Fayette County charges, asserting that denying this credit infringed on his rights under the due process and double jeopardy clauses of the West Virginia Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Circuit Court of Fayette County's order, finding that while the circuit court erred in failing to credit the defendant for the full 263 days, the error was harmless because the defendant ultimately received full credit for time served in Raleigh County.

title: Board of Education v. Cabell County Public Library
description: Whether the Special Acts requiring the Cabell County Board of Education to include funding for the Cabell County Public Library and the Greater Huntington Park and Recreation District on its excess levy proposals violate equal protection guarantees, given that other counties are not subject to such restrictions.
plaintiff_argument: The Board of Education argued that the Special Acts are unconstitutional as they violate equal protection by mandating specific non-school funding on its excess levy proposals, unlike other counties.
defendant_argument: The Library and Park District argued that the Special Acts are constitutional, that the Chafin case insulates excess levies from equal protection review, and that a compelling interest standard does not apply.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's order, ruling that the Special Acts requiring mandatory funding for the Library and Park District on excess levy proposals violate equal protection guarantees and are unenforceable, and that the Board was not required to make equalization payments beyond the specific ballot amounts.

title: State v. Conner
description: Whether the circuit court erred in denying Justin G. Conner's motion for acquittal on his burglary charge, with the plaintiff arguing the defendant waived his arguments and the jury instructions were correct, and the defendant arguing the amended burglary statute requires the dwelling to be 'of another' and he could not burglarize his own home.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Mr. Conner waived his arguments by failing to properly raise them before the circuit court, and that the circuit court's jury instructions correctly included the element of burglary requiring the dwelling to be 'of another person'.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the 2018 amended burglary statute should be interpreted to require the offense to be committed against the dwelling house 'of another', and therefore he could not be convicted of burglarizing his own residence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's denial of Justin G. Conner's motion for a judgment of acquittal of his burglary charge.

title: State v. Horton
description: Whether Adonne A. Horton's life recidivist sentence is unconstitutionally disproportionate under Article III, Section 5 of the West Virginia Constitution, and whether the application of the 2020 version of the recidivist statute violated ex post facto clauses of the West Virginia and United States Constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the life recidivist sentence was constitutional and proportionate because all three of the petitioner's felony offenses involved actual or threatened violence, and the application of the 2020 recidivist statute did not violate ex post facto principles as it did not impose a harsher penalty.
defendant_argument: The petitioner argued that his life recidivist sentence was unconstitutionally disproportionate, especially given his triggering offense, and that applying the 2020 recidivist statute violated ex post facto clauses because it was not in effect at the time of his offense.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia affirmed the circuit court's sentencing order, upholding the petitioner's life imprisonment sentence under the habitual criminal statute.

title: State v. Beaver
description: Whether the Hope Scholarship Act, which provides public funds for non-public education, is constitutional under the West Virginia Constitution's "free schools" clause, which mandates a thorough and efficient system of free public schools.
plaintiff_argument: The Hope Scholarship Act is constitutional because the "free schools" clause does not prohibit the Legislature from enacting additional educational initiatives beyond providing a thorough and efficient system of free schools, and the Act does not impinge on a child's fundamental right to education or improperly direct public funds.
defendant_argument: The Hope Scholarship Act is unconstitutional because the "free schools" clause only permits funding for free public schools, impinges on the fundamental right to education by reducing public school funds, improperly directs public funds to non-public education, usurps the Board of Education's authority, and is a special law.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's order, dissolved the permanent injunction, and remanded the case with directions to enter judgment in favor of the petitioners, thereby finding the Hope Scholarship Act constitutional.

title: State ex rel. West Virginia Secondary School Activities Commission v. Cuomo
description: Whether the West Virginia Secondary School Activities Commission's Residence-Transfer Rule is facially unconstitutional or was applied arbitrarily and capriciously, with the plaintiff arguing it is constitutional and was applied correctly, and the defendant arguing it is unconstitutional and was applied arbitrarily.
plaintiff_argument: The WVSSAC argued that the circuit court lacked jurisdiction to review the as-applied challenge to its Waiver Rule and clearly erred in finding the Residence-Transfer Rule facially unconstitutional, as it is rationally related to a legitimate state purpose and does not violate equal protection.
defendant_argument: Heather B., on behalf of A.B., argued that the WVSSAC's decision to deny a waiver was arbitrary and capricious, and that the Residence-Transfer Rule itself was arbitrary, capricious, and violated equal protection.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia granted the writ of prohibition requested by the WVSSAC and dissolved the circuit court's preliminary injunction.

title: State v. Sheffield
description: Whether the trial court committed reversible error by replacing a deliberating juror with a discharged alternate juror, thereby violating Rule 24(c) of the West Virginia Rules of Criminal Procedure and requiring a new trial.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner argued that the mid-deliberation substitution of a discharged alternate juror violated Rule 24(c) of the West Virginia Rules of Criminal Procedure, creating a presumption of prejudice that the State failed to rebut, thus requiring automatic reversal of his conviction.
defendant_argument: The State argued that any error in the juror substitution was harmless and the petitioner's convictions should be affirmed, as the trial court took adequate precautions to ensure a fair trial.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the petitioner's conviction and sentencing orders and remanded the case for a new trial.

title: Frazier v. Rhodenizer
description: Whether Courtney Rhodenizer suffered actual and substantial prejudice due to a nearly six-year delay in the administrative hearing process, which would justify reversing the revocation of her driver's license.
plaintiff_argument: The DMV argued that Rhodenizer did not sufficiently prove actual and substantial prejudice from the delay, that the DUI was proven, and that she waived her right to a hearing on the delay.
defendant_argument: Rhodenizer argued that she suffered actual and substantial prejudice due to the nearly six-year delay, which violated her due process rights and impacted her livelihood, and that the DMV failed to prove she was DUI.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's decision, reversing the Office of Administrative Hearings' final order and thereby overturning the revocation of Rhodenizer's driver's license.

title: Stepp v. Cottrell
description: Whether claims for excessive force by police officers under the West Virginia Constitution must be analyzed under the specific search and seizure provision (Article III, Section 6) rather than the broader substantive due process clause (Article III, Section 10), and if so, whether claims under Section 10 are redundant when Section 6 claims are also alleged but do not allow for monetary relief.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the West Virginia Constitution provides more protections than the federal Constitution and that a separate cause of action should exist under the general due process clause (Article III, Section 10) for excessive force, especially since monetary damages are foreclosed under Article III, Section 6.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the U.S. Supreme Court's rule (Graham v. Connor) requiring specific constitutional provisions to govern claims should apply to the West Virginia Constitution, meaning excessive force claims should be analyzed under Article III, Section 6 (search and seizure) and not Article III, Section 10 (due process), and that claims under Section 10 would be redundant.
decision_outcome: The court answered both certified questions in the affirmative, holding that claims for excessive force by police officers under the West Virginia Constitution must be analyzed under Article III, Section 6 and not Article III, Section 10, and that claims under Article III, Section 10 are redundant where Article III, Section 6 claims are also alleged but do not allow for monetary relief.

title: In re Goldston
description: Whether Judge Goldston's entry and search of a litigant's home to retrieve marital property constituted a lawful "judicial view" or an unlawful "search" and violated the Code of Judicial Conduct.
plaintiff_argument: The Judicial Disciplinary Counsel argued that Judge Goldston's actions were an unlawful, unconstitutional search and an ethical violation, warranting censure and a $5,000 fine.
defendant_argument: Judge Goldston contended her actions were a lawful "judicial view" or a mere legal error, not an ethical violation, asserting inherent authority to conduct such visits for equitable distribution.
decision_outcome: The court publicly censured Judge Goldston for serious misconduct and ordered her to pay a fine of $1,000.

title: Frazier v. Talbert
description: Whether an officer's failure to comply with West Virginia Code § 17C-5-9 by refusing a DUI suspect's demand for a blood test automatically negates the necessary proof for revoking a driver's license in an administrative proceeding, or if other evidence of aggravated DUI should be considered under a new evaluative test.
plaintiff_argument: The Commissioner argues that the lower tribunals erred by automatically reversing the revocation order based solely on the officer's failure to satisfy respondent's demand for a blood test, without considering other unrebutted evidence of aggravated DUI, and urges the Court to revisit prior decisions to adopt a test that evaluates the violation in the context of the entire record.
defendant_argument: The Respondent counters that his statutory and due process rights were violated when he was denied a blood test, and that the lower tribunals correctly followed precedent in reversing the revocation order, also disputing the Commissioner's claims regarding the validity of the DUI evidence.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's order and remanded the case to the Office of Administrative Hearings for a new hearing, establishing a new three-factor test to evaluate the consequences of denying a blood test in DUI administrative revocation proceedings.

title: State ex rel. AmerisourceBergen Drug Corp. v. Moats
description: Whether defendants in opioid litigation have a right to a jury trial for public nuisance claims and whether the 2015 comparative fault statute applies to these claims.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued that public nuisance claims are equitable, not legal, thus not subject to a jury trial, and that the 2015 Act does not apply to these claims.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued that public nuisance claims are legal, requiring a jury trial, and that the 2015 Act applies, allowing for non-party fault allocation.
decision_outcome: The court denied the writ regarding the applicability of the 2015 Act to public nuisance claims and the denial of a jury trial for public nuisance claims (liability only). However, it granted the writ in part, ruling that if public nuisance claims and legal claims have common issues, a jury must first determine those common issues.

title: State v. Snyder
description: Whether an Emergency Protective Order (EPO) can be considered a de facto search warrant, allowing law enforcement to enter a home and search for firearms without meeting Fourth Amendment probable cause standards.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the EPO itself authorized the entry and search for firearms, or alternatively, that Mr. Snyder implicitly consented to the entry.
defendant_argument: Mr. Snyder argued that the EPO was not a search warrant and the entry and subsequent search of his home violated his Fourth Amendment rights, as no exception to the warrant requirement applied.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's conviction and sentencing order, finding that the EPO did not authorize the search and no warrant exception applied, and remanded the case for further proceedings.
